title: The Usefulness of “Useless Knowledge”
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Kirschner revisits a decade-old post that draws on Abraham Flexner's 1939 essay defending curiosity-driven inquiry. He is prompted by Dutch policy that steers research funding and educational content by popularity and by economic valorisation, and by Sugata Mitra's claim that knowing is obsolete. Using Flexner's Marconi example, he argues that practical breakthroughs rest on theory pursued without any thought of application. He extends this to schooling: knowledge that looks useless is the base for recognising problems, communicating, judging and being creative. Mitra-style arguments, in his view, would take society backwards. The tone is polemical and relies on quotation and analogy, but the line from curiosity and knowledge to creativity and progress is clear.
points: Policy that ties research and curriculum to immediate societal utility or public vote misunderstands where progress comes from.
Flexner's Marconi example shows that applied breakthroughs depend on earlier work done purely out of curiosity.
Knowledge that seems useless is what lets people recognise problems at all, such as global warming.
Creativity is connecting knowledge, so dismissing knowledge as superfluous undermines creativity.
Claims like Mitra's that we need not know until we need to know are presented as a step backwards.
quotes: In other words, the content and approach of the Dutch education system as well as scientific research, would be determined through something similar to a political referendum. Imagine what would happen if we were to do the same for the setup of the national soccer team and their strategy!

According to the Dutch State Secretary for Education the societal “added value” of scientific research must be maximised, which is possible through education, valorisation, and economic applications. In other words, the science and education minister is suggesting that science must be driven by thinking in terms of efficiency and utility.

Flexner explained that all Marconi did was add a final technical detail to what, to that point in time, was pure science. Scientists such as James Maxwell (mathematical calculations on magnetism and electricity) and Heinrich Hertz (theoretical physics research on electromagnetic waves) had laid the foundations for Marconi’s final piece of cake. Maxwell and Hertz did not think “utility” or “application”; they studied ‘stuff’ based on pure curiosity!

Let’s go back to Flexner’s argument, namely that so-called useless knowledge is actually the foundation for further, deeper and more creative thinking. Knowledge that at first glance might be perceived as useless is actually indispensable in that it enables us to book technical/technological, economic, and societal progress. Without such useless knowledge, we wouldn’t even be able to recognise problems; let alone think about them or work towards a solution to them.
Also, last but not least, without this “useless” knowledge, we wouldn’t be able to intellectually communicate about anything. The consequences would be devastating: stagnation and decline.

Steve Jobs said, “Creativity is nothing but connecting things.” Replace the word things with knowledge and it would read: “Creativity is nothing but connecting knowledge.” However, according to many this knowledge is superfluous.
